newsitem.title: USA: Coasts, islands brace for Atlantic hurricanes.
newsitem.headline: Coasts, islands brace for Atlantic hurricanes.

text.p: Memorial Day, the unofficial start of summer, this year heralds for coastal residents a bleaker-than-normal Atlantic hurricane season, six months of torrential rains, deadly winds and pounding waves.

Forecasters expect more tropical storms and hurricanes than average during the 1997 season, prompting Colorado State University professor and weather forecaster Bill Gray to exclaim: "It does not bode very well for the (U.S.) Southeast and the Caribbean."
Memorial Day, celebrated on the last Monday in May as a legal holiday in memory of the dead U.S. servicemen of all wars, marks the imminent start of the hurricane season from June 1 to Nov. 30.

On average since 1950, there have been nine tropical storms a year, of which five or six grow to hurricane strength, with sustained winds of at least 74 mph (118 kph), and two surpass the deadly 110 mph (176 kph) level.

Gray, whose team bases its predictions on an elaborate analysis of the worldwide climate, forecasts 11 tropical storms in the Atlantic and Caribbean in 1997, of which seven will become hurricanes, three intense enough to cause major damage.
Last year there were 13 tropical storms, nine of which became hurricanes, and in 1995 there were 19 tropical storms, 11 of which became hurricanes.
Should the storm forecasts for 1997 prove accurate, the three-year period would be the busiest ever, ushering in what could be decades of increased storm activity.

Despite countless televised scenes of hurricanes tossing boats and cars, blowing over trees, tearing off roofs and leveling houses, forecasters said most residents still fail to take the threat seriously.
They said people do not take precautions ahead of time and only scramble to supermarkets and hardware stores for supplies and protective gear when a storm is just about to hit.
This is true even in Miami, where some areas have not recovered from Hurricane Andrew, which caused some $20 billion in damage when it hit shore five years ago.

"You see the huge lines at Publix (a supermarket chain) when we put up a hurricane watch... you feel like they they didn't really think about it ahead of time," said Jerry Jarrell, deputy director of the National Hurricane Centre.
Precautions might be greater this year in southeastern North Carolina, hit by a rare and cruel double punch in 1996 as Hurricane Bertha stormed onshore in July and was followed by Fran in September.

On Topsail Island, off the North Carolina coast, sewer lines were washed out and water systems ruined as the two storms came ashore. Miles of roads and streets were buried under tons of sand. Power lines and poles were swept away. Houses and businesses were destroyed.

"We lost 25 percent of our rental properties alone, and we're still struggling to establish new setback regulations for building on oceanfront property," said Jeanne Nociti, executive director of the Greater Topsail Area Chamber of Commerce.
While washed-out coastal resorts and flooded Caribbean sugar plantations may be the most familiar images of hurricane damages, emergency workers said inland residents were also affected.

For example, after ploughing ashore in North Carolina in 1996, Fran became the third-costliest storm in U.S. history as it stormed inland and caused flooding all the way to the Great Lakes -- workers sandbagged streets near the White House and Ohio was drenched with six inches of rain.
